This chart shows the dollar exchange rate at today's prices; that is, each past rate has been adjusted for Iran's inflation so it can be compared with today's money. The result is:
• The peak of Mehr and Aban 1397: about 19 thousand tomans, equivalent to 455 thousand tomans today
• In 1399: the rate was about 25 thousand tomans, equivalent to 300 thousand tomans today
• Esfand 1401: the rate of 53 thousand tomans, equivalent to 241 thousand tomans today
So today's dollar, in real terms, is about half the peak of 1397 and roughly at the same level as Esfand 1401 and Khordad 1398. What has happened in these years is mostly the collapse of the rial's value rather than a real rise in the dollar's price. So what matters is the growth of liquidity, not even sanctions and siege!
Big nominal numbers deceive us; the only correct measure is the inflation-adjusted rate.
Important point: the real rate being low compared to historical peaks does not mean the dollar will remain cheap in the future. That is, the recent nominal jumps have only compensated for accumulated inflation, not gone beyond it.

The late Seyyed Mahmoud Taleghani, in the seven months of his life after the 1979 Revolution, enjoyed a popularity beyond imagination. From his words, the general public sensed a suffering, a sincerity, and a purity in which no selfish personal, factional, or ideological motive had any part. Even those segments of the people who were disgruntled with the revolution and loyal to the monarchical system sincerely held him dear and regarded him as being of a different kind. In truth, the late Taleghani was indeed of a different kind. The resonance of his clear voice in the environment of the University of Tehran acted like the blowing of a pleasant and gentle breeze upon hearts fearful and anxious about the fire of the power-seeking conflicts of the age. His voice was full of a spiritual freshness yet accompanied by much sorrow, warning, and deep concern about the future. It was as if he knew what lay ahead. He knew well many of his peers and the various political organizations of that day, and he knew precisely what goal each of them was pursuing behind their pompous and hollow slogans. He did not enter into the game of any of them, nor did he consent to the elimination and exclusion of any of them. He tried to offer a rule for the coexistence of all of them within a pluralist framework, but it was as if he knew how the story would unfold! He concealed his suffering, sorrow, distress, dissatisfaction, and desperation, but it seemed that the poisonous draught of self-consumption and self-restraint wore down his frail and ailing body and took his life. It was as if, in despair of the notables, he sought hope in the masses of the people. He held an optimism and a pleasant feeling toward the common, nameless, and unheralded people. He regarded them as beings endowed with an innate nature (fitrat), and in his view human nature was fashioned from goodness and virtue. Perhaps for this reason, he considered the delegation of the decision-making system to the masses of the people in the form of various councils to be the only path to political salvation. In his view, consultation, deliberation, and the council were the foundation of prophetic politics. For this reason, he insisted firmly on the establishment of councils at all levels of political and social life. In considering the masses of the people as endowed with innate nature, perhaps his own inclinations were also involved. Or perhaps, in his definition of human nature, he had allowed one side of the human species' disposition to dominate the other side more than it should. Whatever it was, it seemed far too idealistic for Iranian society. Perhaps Mr. Taleghani needed to read Plato through the eyes of Strauss, or Hobbes's Leviathan.

Scoring in negotiation (from writings eighteen years ago) One of the rules of giving concessions in a negotiation is that if you give the other party a concession that you thought was valuable and appropriate, and they didn't accept it, or they agreed and then backed out, don't easily give that same concession again later (either give them less, or take more from them, and don't easily go back to the previous agreement). Otherwise, they might not appreciate the concession they receive again. Shopkeepers know this too. For example, when they say they'll give 20% off on something, they give this discount on the condition that the person accepts and buys it right there in the store. But if they say, 'Let me go take a walk and come back,' when they return, either they're told it's sold out, or they say we checked the system and the price is higher, or they say we called the store owner and he said that discount wasn't for this item. It's the same when landing projects. If you tell a client you can do something (at no extra cost) two weeks earlier than the norm, and you see they don't appreciate it and easily pass it by, take a look at your calendar and say, 'I made a mistake.' So they learn to appreciate it when they get a good concession. You might lose out in some places, but in the long run it has many benefits. This rule is followed at all levels of negotiation, from everyday transactions to equations and international relations, and it should be.

Moscow's air temperature was a few degrees higher than St. Petersburg's, but fortunately, it remained at a mild and pleasant level. Sometimes an idea does not die from its first crushing defeat and blow, but from the way its followers choose to resurrect it.
